lines.text: [a long, maniacal laugh trailing off into the intro]
And we're back. Back on the ranch. So this is DVDASA, the ranch series, I guess I'll call it. [beat] Oops, just farted.

So for those of you who don't know, who didn't hear the first episode: basically I've been having a lot of trouble getting work done, focusing, concentrating in the city. So Critter, my sober companion, my confidant, has a friend Sam who owns a ranch in an undisclosed area, and they've been letting me use it. Sam, thank you very much.

This is my third time back to the ranch this month. And while I'm here, I'm painting every day, I'm writing. And because of the overwhelming response to the first blueprint episode, this is going to be a blueprint series within the ranch series.

And as I say that, the first episode hasn't even aired yet, but I'm just guessing people will like it, hopefully. So let's get weird. I might sound a little weird right now, because it's a ranch, it's not the city. I just took a shower where I picked up the soap and a fucking scorpion was behind it.
And I just screamed. I screamed like a little bitch. [laughing] I guess I was a little shocked at my own response to that. The things that make me scream, usually, are rodents. I can't stand them.

And when I woke up this morning I cooked some oatmeal, and what do you know, a fucking little rat, little mouse, just jumped out from under the stove. And I dropped the oatmeal, screamed again like a little bitch.

[shrieking] Aah! They drive me crazy. And then I'd seen a mousetrap outside, so I went out and got it and put a little peanut butter on the end of it. My entire life, most of the places I've lived have been riddled with rodents.

And when I just see the tail, it drives me crazy. So I set the trap, and of course it went off on my fucking finger. Great. So let's get weird. This third time to the ranch. So far the trips have been one week at a time. No phone, no internet, about 200 acres of just nothing around me.

Usually I'm just wearing socks and a cowboy hat, nothing else. But this trip is the one that resembles prison the most — my time in jail in Japan — because it's dark and gloomy, hasn't stopped raining since I got here. So I'm confined, mostly indoors. Not like I really went outside too much anyway, but I'm just stuck in one room for the last few days.

I'm stuck here. And I forgot the power cord to my laptop. I bring my laptop with me — there's no internet here, so it doesn't matter, I don't get any service that way. But what's kept me company on the last two trips has been catching up on Howard Stern episodes, trying to get into BSG, Battlestar Galactica, and listening to music.

And this is most like prison because there's none of that. It's just me in the quiet. There's no music. You know, in a very similar way, people write us and say, hey, I like to listen to DVDASA when I work, and it feels like you guys are my friends.

There's just people talking, filling up the sound while I paint or whatever. But there's none of that this time. So — taking cold showers. Not that there isn't a water heater here, but just to fucking fuck myself up, taking cold showers, getting in the mood. You know, when I was in jail for three months, at the three-month point is when
I started doing a thousand push-ups a day. And people I tell now are like, bullshit. But you've got to understand, it's not like I jumped to a thousand. It was like 100, then 200, then 300.
And when I say I did a thousand push-ups a day, I mean that was basically my entire day. Twenty push-ups, take a break, twenty push-ups, take a break. Get crazy, do forty, and then that's my morning.
Have lunch, then do fifty, do fourteen here, do five here, and just add it up. So right now I'm at a hundred, and hopefully I can get to two hundred before I leave here.
So the feeling, though — I told Critter and the crew when I got home — that one week in solitude, to just create and make art and do whatever you want,

it's amazing. I've been extremely productive, more productive than I've been in months, maybe even years. But the point is, around day six or day seven, when I go home — and this is true for any vacation or anything — one week is the bare minimum of how long it takes for you to forget city life, forget your phone, forget social media.

It's the second week where things really start getting weird. So in that way I was a little disappointed, because every time I got to the point where I started talking to myself and getting super weird is when I'd go home. But things have gotten progressively weirder on this third trip. It's sort of like one week in solitude, then go

home to civilization. It's like being in a low minimum-security prison and getting conjugal visits on the weekend — and I've definitely been taking advantage of the conjugal visits. So let me — I've been keeping notes of what I've been eating and shit, so, since I know you guys are interested, before I jump into this heavy shit —

first of all, first night I got here, I got drunk by myself. And that would be called Drolo, which is drinking solo. Not to be confused with Droon, drinking alone. Or Wasterbation. We all know masturbation is jerking off, having sex by yourself.

Wasterbation is getting wasted by yourself. Drolo — D-R-O-L-O — is drinking solo. Drinking solo is what I did last night. I did not get Droon, which is drunk alone. Not to be confused with Elon, which is eating alone, which I do all the time.

You guys have heard me on the show talk about Brunch, BroFist, and Broner, which is basically most of my life: eating breakfast with the bros, lunch with the bros, or dinner with the bros. Brunch is probably the most important meal of the day.

But up here, and increasingly back home, it's Elon — eating alone. What have I been eating since I've been here? Joe-stadas, basically, is what I ate for breakfast and lunch yesterday and the day before. What is a Joe-stada, you ask? It's sloppy Joe mix on top of a tostada shell

instead of using a hamburger bun, and it is fantastic. I cut a little piece of stinky Roquefort cheese on top, and the best little drizzle of sriracha. The point is, I don't want to spend too much time cooking, I want to create as much art as possible, so I try to make quick things.

So the next thing I made is hot dice, or rice dog. What that is: it's a bed of hot fluffy white rice that I cook, then I put a square sheet of processed orange cheese, like a Kraft single slice, over the rice, and it starts to melt a little. Then I flame-grill a hot dog.

I basically put a hot dog on a chopstick over the stove flame, and it gets all black and starts splitting in half, and then I cut it up and put that over the rice and cheese, and a little swirl of sriracha again — and there you have hot dice, or a rice dog. And then, my back — since I haven't been

painting this long, my hand is starting to cramp up. And I have no use of my laptop, so all my notes and everything I've been writing down for my book is handwritten. So my hand is getting that carpal tunnel feeling, and my back hurts.

So there's this invention my ex-girlfriend made that is amazing. Anyone out there who needs a massage, or whose back hurts, listen up, this is a fucking great one. Basically, you take a tennis ball — a Spalding tennis ball — and you put it in a woman's leg stocking. Don't ask why I have that up here, but I do. And so you have

a tennis ball and a stocking, and you throw that over your shoulder, and then you back into a hard surface, a wall, and just roll your back on the ball. And you adjust the length of the stocking to wherever you have the most pain.
And, you know, as an artist, as anyone who — sorry, I'm gonna blow my nose. [blows nose] Oh shit, blood.

Sorry, a little congested. As anyone who works with their hands or is creative, you need to take breaks and stretch your hand. And if you have someone willing to give you massages, you should get them, they're fucking good for you. And I'm gonna take you a little bit into — I'm just

telling you guys a little about my fucking ranch life before I jump into the blueprint shit, okay, just chill the fuck out. Alright. So, the series of paintings I did in the last two weeks, I'm very happy with. But — I'm being honest with you guys — they're very similar to other things you've seen. And near the end of the second week I started to push

it a little bit more. But for me — you've heard of artists like Andy Warhol, Damien Hirst, Takashi Murakami, who have a factory, they have assistants painting other shit for them. Jeff Koons does this too. And everyone asks me why I don't do that.

I have enough money to pay people to do that. And it's like, are you fucking kidding me? The joy — I don't know, when you're a factory, you're a factory. The joy of creating art — that's the only time that it's the —

it's the point in my life where I'm probably the happiest. Which sounds gay, because it should probably be sex or falling in love. But in the process of making art, there are so many parts — the creating it, the framing it, finding a gallery, or if you're an illustrator, finding someone to sell it for you.

And then the day someone does buy it, or doesn't buy it. There's a lot of emotion that goes along with making art and trying to sell it. So the part that's the best, to me, is not the selling and making lots of money.
It's the actual creation of it. So to have a factory, or have someone come in and paint my shit for me — I mean, why would I pay someone to take that joy away from me?
It's the most therapeutic thing. For someone like me, who talks so fucking much and used to have three therapists and this radio show and an amazing group of friends to talk to constantly,

you'd think I'd have nothing left to say. But there's always still more to say. And sometimes you can't find the words, and to just express it through paint is the best. So I'm gonna take you through my pretentious pigment-pushing process.
And it is. And I know, as I explain this process, I'm gonna sound like a fag, and you're gonna be like, what the fuck is this guy talking about? But just come along with me.

And just ask yourself out there why you make art. There are people who make art because they just enjoy creating; they're not trying to push the envelope, they're not trying to be really innovative. But you need to ask yourself these questions — like why you even make art in the first place. So for me, I say, why make art unless you're going to go all the way?
Sometimes I'll just be painting, and in the middle of it frustration hits me so hard, just because it's like — what is this? What am I adding to anything? You know?
For me it's an exploration. In a world where you go see a preview for a movie and you fucking know how it's gonna end —

you already saw the best parts in the preview. Or relationships. Most of the time, you know how shit's gonna go down. For the most part you know how movies are gonna end, you know how things are gonna happen, and it's very rare that you're surprised. So for me, with art, even though I'm the one creating it, I love surprising myself.

You know, like the Stranger — when you sit on your hand till it's numb, freeze it, and then you jerk yourself off so it feels like a stranger's doing it? You guys know the Stranger. I like doing that with art. So I'm out here on the ranch, 200 acres of nothing, there's no one around.
It's a fucking scorpion and a goddamn little mouse. [shouting] Fuck you! So besides the scorpion and the mouse, it's just me. And so this is it. I made the moves and the effort to come here.
So why not fucking get weird? Why not go push it all the way? So I did. Critter's truck was full of canvases. I painted all of them. So we hit the art store again before we came out here.
And I bought a bunch of gel mediums so I could make my own paints while I'm out here. So the first thing I did — there's no reference. I don't want to use any reference.
I don't like to sketch anything out. I want to keep it as raw as possible. I've drawn enough landscapes, women, cities, animals — I know how to draw, okay. It doesn't have to look perfect.
Like, one of the conversations I had with Critter on the way home last trip — he has an art show coming up with my mom — and he said, Dave, I'm having a real tough time painting noses.
And I said, why don't you just not paint noses then? Or just paint a triangle. Or I don't know — if you're having a tough time, and it's art, do whatever the fuck you want.

[mock voice] You'll be the guy that doesn't paint noses on his people. And he's like, just don't paint it? I'm like, yeah. Sorry — what I'm going for here is raw, and it's pure. That's the point I'm trying to get to. So: no painting for three days. For 72 hours I deprived myself of sleep. And I didn't sleep

the night before either, so I counted that. And no ejaculation, no self-love. So three days, 72 hours, walking around in a sort of spirit quest — an erection quest, if you will — in a dream state. I'm extremely exhausted. I'm tired. And because there's no sound out here, there's no music, no television, no YouTube, no nothing.
You can finally hear yourself think. I see people read or do stuff while listening to music. I can't. Some of the best art I've ever done,
I wasn't listening to music. Even jogging — people jog and listen to music to get inspired, kill time. But when you jog without any music, you can hear your breath.
You notice everything you're running past. So I said, I'm going to choose to — at 72 hours is when you start to feel like you're on drugs.
So my third day, I deprived myself of sleep. And during that time I laid out all the canvases around the living room, like they were my friends.
And I'd just look at them, and there's nothing there. They're just blank white canvases. There's nothing. It's abstract. They're just blank. They're newborn babies.
And for those of you who listen to the show, you know I don't shower much and I don't really brush my teeth, so I have really bad breath. And sometimes spit flies out when I talk.
So over the course of the three days, even though they're just blank canvases, they start to take on different personalities. Like the one next to the door was a dickhead. I don't know.

For whatever reason, I just didn't like him. The one closest to me on the couch was a girl, and I liked her, and she was very sweet to me. And so, the way humans personalize everything, these became my buddies and some of them my enemies.

So I would scream at them sometimes, talk to them, my bad breath getting all over the canvas. When I'd eat, I'd eat on top of them. When I went to the bathroom, I'd take one with me and just leave it in front of me while I shit. And I'd just stare at

it. And so on the third day — this is three days without making any marks on them, just leaving them alone, studying them — on the third day, I had pre-cum coming out of my pants, because for those of you listening to the show, you know I jerk off at least once, or three times, a day.

And to go three days without — I had a huge load, so I shot all my gel mediums out a little bit and I shot a huge load into all my paints. And then, just walking outside in the rain, I started collecting leaves and pine cones and weird mushrooms and shit I found outside.
And I grinded them up using a rock. And that was very therapeutic, to have these things I found outside. And I mixed all these into the pigments and made my own paint, basically.
So with no references — I don't know if you've watched Ghostbusters, when the Stay Puft Marshmallow Man comes. That happened because Ray thought of the fucking Stay Puft Marshmallow Man.

And when Gozer said, choose your death, or whatever the fuck it said — you had to clear your mind of anything. You had to make your mind blank. And I remember, as a kid watching Ghostbusters, going: the more you try not to think of something, something keeps popping up.

So basically Ghostbusters was Zen. And I've spent an entire life training myself to try to get to a point where you can think of nothing. When I see people meditating or praying or doing any of these things, I'm impressed, because I want to get to that point — I mean, can you just think of nothing?
So that's what I was trying to get to. On the third day I wanted my mind to be clear. And then I just fucking attacked the canvas. I attack it. It's so violent.
And it's full of so much emotion, so much — it's pure, pure expression. To the point where I start crying sometimes. I know, super gay, but what can I say? I'm being honest with you.
And the three days previous, I'm in almost a meditative state. There are no marks on the canvas, like I said. And over and over again I imagine what I'm going to paint, what it's going to look like.
And then I try to not — I want to be conscious of it — I basically want to elevate my consciousness to a point where I stop doing that, because that's planning.
But I'm confident of my skills. So I'm performing this mental karate in my head, it's just a buildup, it's — what do you call it? — foreplay before the big show.

So then on the third day I just attack. I spit, I slap, I'm crying, I'm screaming, I'm just ripping at these with all the paint, all the colors. And like I said, I start crying. And then I notice — you know, people

know I made fun of Bobby Lee for taking a selfie of himself while he's crying. But in a place like this, in solitude by myself, as I'm painting and I start crying, I realize how fucking gay this is. And so there's a big mess. Now it looks like a murder scene. Now

there are canvases like dead bodies. Three days ago they were newborn babies. Now they're just murder victims. And they're strewn all over the fucking ranch. And some of them, while they're still wet, I finally go, I'm gonna sleep now. And I sleep with them. Some of them I sleep on top of. Some of them, I bring my own sheets and I just

hug them and spoon them and sleep with the canvas. And of course I wake up and it looks like you fucked a chick on her period. And the really wet ones, I wake up and I'm sort of stuck to them. But now I've spent a lot of time with these paintings. A lot of emotion has gone
into them. And the next morning I wake up, they're dry. I take them outside and line them up, and in front of each one I get on my knees, I kneel before it and I say, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

I'm sorry. And I ask each painting for forgiveness. I beg. I humble myself to the painting, to the process of this art-making, and I beg the fucking painting for forgiveness for hours. I'm sorry. Like Steve Lee, who loves Drew Barrymore and would say to himself into a tape

recorder, [imitating Steve Lee] I love you, Drew Barrymore, I love you, Drew Barrymore — I'm sitting up here, and I guess hearing Steve say that brought back all my OCD tendencies. I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I don't even know what the fuck I'm sorry for, I just know I'm begging this fucking piece of canvas for forgiveness. And the abstract marks and squiggles and shapes

all over it — I see them, and they start changing. And people always ask me, how long did that painting take you? Because I try not to put thought into it, I just try to go stream of consciousness, the same way I do the show and the same way I write.

And most paintings — the actual painting part — take me less than a day to do. But what people don't understand is all the shit I'm telling you: it's an entire life of training for this moment. Like a boxing match that takes twelve rounds,

less than an hour or whatever — these boxers spend their entire lives getting their bodies in shape for this. So in the same way, all this training I've done, to make these confident, sure, swift, masterful strokes — people are like, come on, just paint it in a second, it'll take you two seconds. Yeah, it'll take me two seconds, but I spent my life preparing

for this. And so after I apologize to the paintings, I take a black gesso and I paint over either the entire painting or just parts of it. And I start all over again. I bring in a bunch of layers, just like a human being is not so simple. We're

very hypocritical, multilayered, contradicting personalities. I try to capture all that. And even if you paint over the black, there's something underneath that. It's like when you see someone who's really quiet — they're not talking, but there's something going on there. So the ones that I don't

paint over entirely, I bring out shapes to the foreground, the forefront. And the shapes that seem the most aesthetic and desirable, I just deface them and push them back into the abyss. And that's how I paint out here. And I know a lot of artists
are like, yeah, Dave's a crazy artist, this and that, I wish I could paint like that. To you, I say this. When I was in high school, I ran faster than any black kid at my school.

And people were like, [mock voice] look at that little chink motherfucker. Because they didn't understand it — we're talking about six-foot-five dudes who just run — I mean, they could probably run faster than me now. But I would just imagine the police chasing me, and I'd been chased a few times before,

and the disappointment of my parents, and I'm just running around a track. But these are all the things I would think. So if there's anyone out there — oh yeah, so I'm imagining the police chasing me.
And that just lit an insane fire, and I would explode. So in the same way, if you're having trouble as an artist — you have a creative roadblock in your head and

you're like, man, I wish I could take those kinds of chances — it's a fucking goddamn painting. Okay? I'm sitting here talking about worshipping it and apologizing to it. It's a fucking inanimate thing. It's everything and it's nothing.
You understand what I'm saying? It has the power to change people and bring out emotion and inspire. And at the same time, it's nothing. It's literally not a human being.
It's just a fucking thing. It's an object. So don't be scared. And if you want to challenge yourself, if you're a scared fucking artist right now, I say this to you.
If you're a scared pussy and you don't want to be one, and you want to paint with confidence and push yourself — imagine a man holding a gun to your head right now.

And imagine a man holding a gun to your family, or whoever you love the most — your dog, your wife, your brother, your sister, your mom or dad — whoever, the person you love the most is sitting in front of you, and you have a canvas in front of you.
And he says, in fifteen minutes I'm going to blow your dog's brains out. You'd better paint the most amazing painting. It doesn't have to be a painting of your dog — it can be.

And I guarantee you, whatever painting you paint in those fifteen minutes, with the threat of your dog about to die, will be maybe the greatest painting you've ever painted. You hear it over and over with these pop stars — they're like, how did you write, you know, 'Louie Louie'

or whatever — and they go, [mock voice] oh, divine inspiration hit me, and I wrote it in ten minutes, fifteen minutes. So you want manufactured inspiration? How about fucking fear? How about the most loved person in your life having their brains exploded in front of your face if you don't paint the best fucking thing?
So try that as an exercise, as a test. So let's get into this shit. Thanks for listening so far.
So let's start with failure. The anger, the negativity, holding onto suffering and regret. Failure — it's just part of life. We fail at so many things. We fail our driver's license test.

We fail in relationships. We fail at things. And you're so angry. I don't play sports, but I can only imagine being in the Super Bowl, or any sport with that level of pressure, and you caught the touchdown but it just fumbled, or it just touched the tip of your fingertips and you dropped it, or you missed the field goal that would have won the game.
And you go back to your city and everyone's booing you, and you want to contemplate suicide, and you suck, you're fucking horrible.
That's part of life. And when you have something you fail that hard at, it's easy to hold onto that suffering and regret and stay in that angry, negative place. But this is for fucking idiots.

Whenever you meet people who are just angry all the time, they're fucking idiots. It's dumb. It's not smart. If you're an intelligent person, you'll see the big picture, and you'll understand that these failures are a fucking gift to you.
You don't learn anything with success. When you're successful, all it does is feed your ego and you think you're the fucking man. [cocky voice] I knew it. I'm a fucking god. I'm the fucking man.

I know everything. I'm perfect. Every time I do anything — touchdown. You don't learn anything. All it does is turn you into a fucking shithead. Failures humble you, teach you. Of course you're going to feel regret.
Of course you're going to be sad. Let it go. Don't be stupid. Don't be a fucking idiot.
So first of all, to fail — now you know failure is a gift, the greatest gift. Now, to fail, you must — the first thing you have to do is you've got to fucking get yourself out there.
How are you going to fail and get rejected by a girl if you never ask a girl? How are you going to miss the touchdown if you never join the team? Get in the fucking game.

Okay? To fail, to have the opportunity, to have this gift, this present of failure, you have to fucking go to the dance. So get up, brush yourself off, put a nice fucking suit on — a nice burgundy corduroy suit — comb your hair, and get to the fucking dance.

Okay, and try. You don't know what's gonna happen, you've never been there before, you don't like to dance — but you have to. To get the reward, you have to risk it. And to even have the opportunity to fail, you have to fucking go there. I don't know how the fuck people are going to like

me talking about how to live their lives, but I'm doing it anyway. People might hate this shit. People might be like, you're a fucking idiot. And they did, actually. I dropped out of art school, and I went back to my mentor, Baron Storey, at CCAC — or I guess it's just CCA now — in Oakland.

And I sat in the back of the class, because I love his demonstrations and I love watching him draw and I just wanted to watch. And he said, oh look, one of my old students, David Choe, is here, come talk to the class. And I'd been out of art school for two years by then, and I was getting

my art out there in Vice magazine, Giant Robot, little things here and there. And I told everyone to just drop out, and I started spurting off at the mouth, as I always do, all this — do this, do this. And then Baron took me aside at the end of class and said, look, I didn't
ask you to speak in front of my class to tell them all to drop out of school. That worked out for you, but you're giving really dangerous advice.
So I might be doing that again right now. This might be horrible advice for someone. But just see if it resonates with you.
So, you know, I brag often about how — most people found out about me through my Facebook deal, where they're like, it's like you won the lotto.

And that really bothered me for a long time. It shit on every accomplishment I'd done up until that point, and it really disappointed me. They're like, oh, he's rich now, and he gets to fuck all these girls and sell his art for this much

and whatever. It's like, motherfucker — I'd made millions gambling, I'd made millions off my art, and I'd already been having sex with beautiful women before any of that. But no one gives a shit, no one wanted to hear that. So I'd become a millionaire three times over, in three different ways — through art, gambling, and Facebook. So they're like, this guy

isn't no failure, he's fucking awesome, he just makes money no matter what he does. Which is actually sort of true. And so, to debunk that a little bit, I'll take you through a list of my failures, which is pretty endless. I'll take you through some of the most epic ones.

I'll take you back — since it's a Friday right now, flashback Friday — back to the gambling. This is one, and you want to talk about regret, this is one I couldn't let go of for almost a year, maybe years even.
I'd entered a Baccarat tournament in Las Vegas. I won't say which hotel. This is a $2.5 million tournament. You have to be an extremely good player to get into it.

There are probably 200 players. So basically you have a one-in-200 chance to become a millionaire, which is pretty fucking good. And you're playing with extremely, extremely rich people. Tournament play — people know about poker tournaments, but blackjack tournaments, roulette tournaments, it's a whole other thing.

You're basically playing to get as many chips as possible. But it's a weird game, because you make secret bets, so you don't know what people are betting. You just have to be the highest earner at the table — but people could be going all in and you wouldn't know, because of all these secret bets.
With that being said, I made it through the quarterfinals. I destroyed the semifinals. And all you had to do was make it to the finals, and then you'd cash out.

Basically, twelfth place even made like fifty grand. It was fifty, sixty grand. And then first place — I think second place got like 900,000, and first place got one-point-something million. So I knew I could do it. I'd been killing it. I'd been playing for three days straight. For those of you who know Johnny Chan, he's a poker player — he also fucking plays Baccarat.
And I had all the money. Basically at the semifinals I had the most money of anyone at the table. And then the last bet is the secret bet.
And if I had — I just don't know what happened. And, to quote this, if this is a sport, this is like the World Series. My secret bet was sixty-six thousand dollars.

And all the people who had less money than me, they were going all in. But it didn't matter. With 66, if I lost the bet on bank, I'd still win. And if I put it on player and I won, all the people going all in on player — I'd still win.

So it was the perfect amount. I did the math, which I suck at, on a piece of paper, and that was it. And then when they opened up my secret bet, they go, David Choe bets sixty-six hundred. I was like, no, no, no, no — sixty-six thousand.
And they're like, oh, you forgot a zero. Me forgetting that zero cost me this — this would have been — I was a young man then, this is probably five, six, seven years ago.

Let's see, I'm 37 — eight years ago, this would have been eight years ago. And oh my god, I asked the judges, I said, listen, here's the math I did on this other piece of paper, what I meant — and they're like, look, we know that you meant sixty-six thousand, but it's tournament rules, sorry. And so

the blood filled to my face. I was 29 years old, and I was about to become a millionaire through fucking gambling — or at least have a one-in-twelve chance. I was right there at the final table. At least I could have made fucking fifty grand

if I'd played the shittiest. And the blood — I thought my head was going to explode, I thought I was going to faint. I fucking went outside, and like an insane person, I didn't stop screaming that loud for days. Every time I thought about it, I wanted to kill

myself. I couldn't believe I'd done so good in the tournament — to even get in it, to be asked, it was invitational only — and then to have odds like that, and to just gooch it, just fuck it up over writing, not writing, the one extra fucking zero. I should slow down, I'm getting upset
